summary: Defines WebDAV, a set of methods, headers, and content types added to HTTP/1.1 for managing resource properties, creating and organizing collections, moving things around in the URL space, and locking to avoid edit collisions. It obsoletes RFC 2518 with minor revisions. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Normal web pages are mostly for reading. WebDAV lets people edit files on a web server together and take turns, like a shared folder.

questions: what is the difference between propfind and proppatch
subtitle: HTTP extensions that let clients edit, organise and lock files on a web server instead of only reading them.

tldr.problem: Plain HTTP is good at fetching pages but gives clients no standard way to manage properties, build folders, copy or move resources, or stop two authors overwriting each other.
tldr.mechanism: WebDAV adds methods (PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, MKCOL, COPY, MOVE, LOCK, UNLOCK), headers (DAV, Depth, Destination, If, Lock-Token, Overwrite, Timeout), XML request and response bodies, and a 207 Multi-Status response.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4918 obsoletes RFC 2518 with minor revisions mostly due to interoperability experience, and has been updated by RFC 5689.

today: RFC 4918 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2518 and has been updated by RFC 5689.

sections.title: What WebDAV Adds to HTTP
sections.content:
WebDAV is an extension to HTTP/1.1 that lets clients perform remote Web content authoring. It provides four groups of operations:

  • Properties: create, remove and query information about pages, such as authors and creation dates.
  • Collections: create sets of documents and retrieve a hierarchical membership listing, like a directory listing.
  • Locking: keep more than one person from working on a document at once, preventing the lost update problem.
  • Namespace operations: ask the server to copy and move resources, which changes the mapping from URLs to resources.

The versioning operations suggested by RFC 2291 are not part of this document; they are in RFC 3253. This RFC obsoletes RFC 2518, published in February 1999.
sections.eli5: The web is like a library where you can only borrow books. WebDAV adds a way to write in them, make new shelves, move books around and put a 'being used' sign on one.

sections.title: Properties and Collections
sections.content:
A property is a name and value pair describing a resource, for example a subject or an author. The value is always a well-formed XML fragment. Live properties have their syntax and meaning enforced by the server (for example DAV:getcontentlength). Dead properties are only recorded verbatim by the server, and the client keeps them consistent.

A collection is a resource that also acts as a container, modelling things like file system directories. It holds mappings from path segments to resources, and it MUST contain at most one mapping for a given path segment. When a method could apply to members, the client sets a depth: zero levels (only the collection), one level (the collection and directly contained resources), or infinite levels.

By convention a server MAY treat a collection URL without a trailing slash as if it had one, and SHOULD then return a Content-Location header. Clients are better off checking the DAV:resourcetype property than guessing from the URL.
sections.eli5: A property is a sticky note on a file saying who wrote it. A collection is a folder, and you can say whether you mean just the folder, what is directly inside it, or everything inside all the way down.

sections.title: The New Methods
sections.content:
WebDAV defines these methods, and all DAV-compliant resources MUST support PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, COPY and MOVE:

  • PROPFIND retrieves properties. The client MUST send a Depth header of 0, 1 or infinity. The body can name properties, ask for allprop (which does not return every live property) or ask for propname (just the names). An empty body is treated as allprop.
  • PROPPATCH sets and removes properties. Instructions are processed in document order and either all succeed or none do.
  • MKCOL creates a collection. It fails if the URL is already mapped, and fails with 409 if the parent does not exist.
  • COPY and MOVE use a Destination header. The Overwrite header is T or F and defaults to T; if it is F and the destination exists, the method fails with 412. MOVE is a copy, consistency maintenance and delete performed as one operation.
  • LOCK and UNLOCK take out, refresh and release locks.

PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, MKCOL, COPY and MOVE are described as idempotent but not safe, except PROPFIND, which is both safe and idempotent.
sections.eli5: These are new verbs for talking to the server: 'tell me about this file', 'change the note on this file', 'make a folder', 'copy this', 'move this', 'lock this', 'unlock this'.

sections.title: Locking
sections.content:
A lock serializes access to a resource so an authoring client can reasonably expect no one else will change it while it is being edited. Locks come in two scopes. An exclusive lock conflicts with any other lock on the same resource. A shared lock lets several principals hold a lock at once, so collaborators can see who else may be working on it; each gets their own lock and token. Only the write lock type is defined here.

Each lock has exactly one globally unique lock token, which clients MUST NOT try to interpret and submit in an If header. A LOCK with Depth: infinity on a collection locks all members and returns one token; either the whole hierarchy is locked or none of it is. A lock may have a timeout in seconds, but clients MUST assume locks can disappear at any time. A lock is refreshed by an explicit LOCK request with no body.

Support for locking is optional. The RFC admits locks cannot prevent every lost update: an ordinary HTTP client that never locks can still overwrite a locked document, because WebDAV cannot force all clients to lock.
sections.eli5: A lock is like putting your name on a whiteboard next to a document so others wait their turn. It only works if everybody looks at the whiteboard, and the sign can fall off.

sections.title: Multi-Status Responses and New Status Codes
sections.content:
Because one request can touch many resources, WebDAV adds the 207 Multi-Status response. Its body is XML with a multistatus root holding zero or more response elements, each with an href and either a status or, for PROPFIND and PROPPATCH, one or more propstat elements giving the status of individual properties. The overall 207 does not say whether the operation worked; the client must read the body.

Four other codes are added: 422 Unprocessable Entity (well-formed but semantically wrong XML), 423 Locked, 424 Failed Dependency and 507 Insufficient Storage. Error bodies can carry named precondition and postcondition XML elements such as lock-token-submitted or no-conflicting-lock.
sections.eli5: When you ask the server to do many things at once, it sends back a report card listing what worked and what did not for each item, instead of a single yes or no.

sections.title: Compliance Classes
sections.content: A resource advertises what it supports in the DAV header of an OPTIONS response. A class 1 resource meets all the MUST requirements and returns at least 1. A class 2 resource also supports LOCK, the DAV:supportedlock and DAV:lockdiscovery properties and the lock headers, and returns at least 1 and 2. A class 3 resource advertises support for the revisions made in this document to RFC 2518, and class 1 must be supported as well. Compliance is described per resource, not per server.
sections.eli5: Class 1 means 'I can do the basics'. Class 2 adds 'and I can do locks'. Class 3 means 'I follow the newest edition of the rules'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because WebDAV is about writing, authentication protects the integrity of resources, not just access. Basic authentication MUST NOT be used unless the connection is secure, and WebDAV applications MUST support Digest authentication (RFC 2617).

Other risks the RFC lists: denial of service (huge PUTs, recursive operations on large collections, many pipelined requests); PROPFIND listing members, which weakens security through obscurity; owner contact information in DAV:lockdiscovery and author data in properties, which can be private; XML external and nested internal entities; version 1 UUID lock tokens that can expose an IEEE 802 address; and users publishing malicious content to the server.
sections.eli5: Letting strangers change files needs a strong lock on the door. Passwords must not be shouted across an open room, and the server must not trust tricky files that other people upload.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2518
sections.content:
Appendix F lists the changes. Servers advertise them all by returning compliance class 3. Notable ones:

  • allprop was relaxed to return the defined live properties at minimum, with a new include element to ask for more.
  • Servers may now reject PROPFIND with Depth: infinity, and clients must now send a Depth header on PROPFIND.
  • Multi-Status gained a location element and an error element.
  • Lock-null resources were replaced by simpler locked empty resources, and there is no implicit lock refresh anymore.
  • A DAV:lockroot element lets clients find the root of a lock.
  • UTF-16 support in XML bodies is now required.
sections.eli5: After people tried the first edition in real life, the authors fixed the confusing parts, so different programs would work together better.

items.label: Read properties
items.desc: Needs a Depth header of 0, 1 or infinity.

items.label: Change properties
items.desc: All instructions succeed or none do.

items.label: Make collection
items.desc: Fails with 409 if the parent is missing.

items.label: Relocate
items.desc: Copy plus delete in one operation.

items.label: Release a lock
items.desc: Deletes the lock with the given token.

viz.caption: CODES ADDED TO HTTP/1.1 BY WEBDAV

items.title: 207 Multi-Status
items.text: Status for several independent operations, read from the XML body.

items.title: 422 Unprocessable Entity
items.text: Well-formed request, but the instructions cannot be processed.

items.title: 423 Locked
items.text: The source or destination resource is locked.

items.title: 424 Failed Dependency
items.text: An action this one depended on failed.

items.title: 507 Insufficient Storage
items.text: The server cannot store what the request needs.
